LeakTrace

Tracing leaked exam papers to the printing centre with invisible layout fingerprints · SDG 4 (Quality Education) · research-prototype report · English & Hindi
Investigative lead, not proof. LeakTrace estimates which centre's printed copy a photographed paper came from. It does not show who leaked it, and a retyped paper carries no fingerprint (tested, §4.5). All accuracy figures below are from a physical-channel simulation (rendered pages → modelled printer → modelled camera/messaging). The real printed-and-photographed study and the human visibility study have not been run; both are built and documented (§5) and are the next step.

Summary

What was built. A typesetting engine that gives each centre's copy a keyed pattern of tiny word-gap and line-position shifts (default ±0.30 pt, provisional); a deterministic decoder (OCR only locates words; no learned model decides) that takes a degraded, cropped photo and scores every centre against the unmodified master, reports a wrong-key-calibrated p-value, and rejects photos without a valid fingerprint; a degradation simulator; five experiments; a FastAPI + React app (paper preparation, investigation dashboard with overlay); a reader-study kit and a real-photo protocol. 11 automated tests pass.
Headline results (simulation). Full-page photos: 319/320 correct and accepted across 20 degradation/printer/paper-warp conditions (Wilson 95% CI 98.3–99.9%), 0 wrong accepts; false accepts on plain pages 0/120 and on valid copies of unlisted centres 0/40. Partial leaks: at α=10-3 over 200 centres a photo needs about 4 text lines at phone quality (25/28 correct at 4 lines, pooled over two runs; CI 73–96%) and about 20 lines for a low-resolution WhatsApp-compressed image — where the limit is OCR/alignment, not the fingerprint. A header serial or 2 cm QR code, read perfectly on clean whole pages, was recovered from only 0–29% (header) and 0–14% (QR) of the same random crop windows. Hindi matches English on full pages; short Hindi crops fall below the significance floor sooner. Added random jitter ≤0.4 pt, rescaling, JPEG q15, sharpening and 90°/180° rotation do not defeat it; ≥0.8 pt jitter and retyping do.
What is not established. Whether ±0.30 pt (or any value) is unnoticeable to people (E1 human half); how a real laser printer, real paper and real phones perform; the offset size to ship.

1 Problem, scope and threat model

When a paper leaks, authorities can cancel and re-run the exam, but tracing the origin is slow and honest candidates pay for the retest. Visible marks (serials, QR codes, headers) are cropped out, and digital watermarks do not survive a phone photo of printed paper that a messaging app has resized and compressed. LeakTrace instead hides the identity in the layout: sub-point shifts of word gaps and line positions that are repeated across the whole page, so a crop to a few lines still carries them.

Setting. Authorities hold the unmodified master M, a secret key k and N centres; the decoder is non-blind (it compares against M). Adversary and channel: phone photo (perspective, blur, resizing, JPEG/WhatsApp), partial view, rotation/rescaling, collusion of copies, added jitter, or retyping. Out of scope: proving individual guilt, leaks of the digital master before printing, papers whose layout we did not typeset.

2 Method

2.1 Embedding

The paper is typeset with WeasyPrint (HarfBuzz shaping, so Devanagari conjuncts are correct) with every word in its own span. The master is the normal flow layout; a centre's copy is the identical HTML with position:relative; left:dx; top:dy on selected spans, which moves ink without touching line breaking or justification. Word/line boxes are read from the laid-out box tree and stored as the master layout JSON. A centre seed is HMAC-SHA256(k, "centre:"+id); keyed bits are drawn per (page, line) from the same HMAC. Gap channel: the gaps of a line are paired (0,1),(2,3),…; a pair gets (+s,−s)·δ, i.e. exactly one word moves by ±δ and the line width, hence the justified margins, is unchanged (verified by test). An odd last gap is unmarked. Line channel: consecutive lines are paired and moved (+s,−s)·ε vertically, so a global vertical shift of a photo cannot masquerade as a fingerprint. The fingerprint is repeated on every line of every page. Embedding is exact: the PDF read-back shows displacements of {−0.30, 0, +0.30} pt with no re-shaping.

Capacity. The English master has 1056 words, 86 lines, 930 marked gaps and 86 marked lines over 3 pages (Hindi: 1088 words, 86 lines, 956 / 86). Because signs come in pairs, information is one independent bit per pair — about 508 bits for the whole paper and ≈ 5 bits per text line. This drives the partial-leak floor (§4.3).

2.2 Decoding

Steps: (1) illumination flattening and Tesseract word boxes (eng or hin+eng) — OCR is used only to find where words are; (2) tokens are matched to the master by sequence alignment (script-tolerant skeletons), the page is voted, a homography (affine for few anchors) is fitted with RANSAC; (3) the photo is rectified to the master raster at 4 px/pt, the master is blurred to the photo's estimated sharpness, and each word's sub-pixel displacement is measured by ECC translation on a tight word patch; a robust low-order residual trend (affine, quadratic with ≥160 words) absorbs lens/paper distortion; (4) the offset at gap j is rj = (dxk+1−dxk)/δ and at line j the weighted mean dy/ε, clipped to ±2; quality qj ∈ [0,1] comes from the ECC correlation of the words involved; (5) for every centre T(c) = Σ qj sj(c) rj / Σ qj.

Decision. The null distribution is the same statistic computed on the same measurements with 4000 wrong keys (random unlisted centre ids). The single-centre p-value is empirical when at least 5 null scores exceed it and a Gaussian-tail extrapolation otherwise; it is multiplied by N (Bonferroni). The photo is accepted only if the family-wise p < α (default 10-3) and enough marked positions were measured; otherwise it is rejected and nothing is inferred. Reported confidence is 1−p, with the margin to the runner-up in null σ. Several significant centres are returned as a candidate set (collusion). If the upright page is unreadable the decoder tries 90/180/270° rotations. Significance floor: for a noise-free match with B independent bits, z ≈ √B; accepting at α=10-3 over N=200 needs z ≥ Φ-1(1−α/N) = 4.4, i.e. B ≥ 19.4 bits ≈ 39 marked gaps ≈ 4 lines.

2.3 Reproducibility and tests

Python 3.13, pinned requirements.txt, fixed seed (20261031), one make target per stage; every trial is stored as JSONL. Experiments use a key different from the one used while building the decoder. Tests: key→sign determinism and independence, exact embedded offsets, justified margins preserved, no re-shaping, embed→decode round trip on 10 centres with no degradation (100%), score grows with visible lines, accuracy does not improve with more blur, plain pages and non-paper images rejected, Hindi shaping preserved, and an end-to-end API test (prepare → photo → decode → overlay; wrong key rejected).

3 Experimental setup

Mock papers written for this project (English and Hindi, 40 questions each, 3 pages). N=200 candidate centres (code supports 5000). Photo simulator: perspective, rotation, defocus/motion blur, resize, lighting (gradient, vignette, gamma), sensor noise, JPEG, crop to a region or to n text lines, and a WhatsApp step (long side ≤1600 px, JPEG q72). Physical-channel models added after a first run came out too good: a laser-printer model (page rasterised to bilevel dots at 150–1200 dpi, then photographed; E3–E5 use 600 dpi), per-word placement noise (0.05 pt default), non-rigid paper warp, and smooth paper-feed error. Trials per cell are 8–16, so confidence intervals are wide; Wilson 95% intervals are shown. Trials draw copies from a pool of 30 centres per language but score against all 200.

4 Results

4.1 E1 — Visibility

Objective half (done). SSIM between the plain page and a fingerprinted page, restricted to text-line regions at 4 px/pt, falls from 0.98–1.00 (δ=0.05 pt) through 0.91 (δ=0.30, English) / 0.87 (Hindi) to 0.77 / 0.65 at 1.0 pt (Fig. 1); at δ=0.30 about 9–11% of text-line pixels change by more than 16 grey levels. SSIM and pixel change are proxies: they say the page changed, not whether a reader notices.

Human half (kit built, not run). eval/reader_study.py produces a self-contained HTML study (56 two-alternative forced-choice trials, English and Hindi × 7 offset levels × 4 repetitions, randomised sides, real size, anonymous, results downloaded as CSV), an answer key, a printable PNG set for the print variant, and an analysis script that reports accuracy per level with Wilson intervals and an exact binomial test against chance, and picks the largest unnoticed δ. It needs ≥20 volunteers and instructor approval. Until it is run, δ=ε=0.30 pt is an engineering default with no visibility evidence behind it.

Finding. The simulator (E2b below) decodes at offsets as small as 0.05 pt, so detectability is not what limits δ; visibility is. The study should therefore pick the smallest offset that keeps comfortable margin on real prints, not the largest invisible one.

False accept. 0/120 plain-page photos and 0/40 valid copies of centres not on the list were accepted (upper 95% bounds 3.1% and 8.8%). With these sample sizes the design level α=10-3 cannot be verified empirically; it follows from the wrong-key null (median best-of-200 z on plain pages was 2.67, i.e. no inflation visible).

Channel ablation (same measurements, three scorers; table above). The gap channel alone identifies everything the combined decoder does; the line channel alone carries only one bit per pair of lines (≈14 bits per page) and cannot reach α=10-3 over 200 centres from one page — its top-1 is shown in the table. It still ranks the correct centre first in 98% of full-page trials (table), but in simulation it adds nothing the gap channel does not already provide; since it is itself a visible change it could be dropped unless real photos show the gap channel to be unreliable.

Header-only mark baseline (serial in the page header on every page, read by the same OCR) and QR baseline (2 cm code, either OpenCV or zxing counts) on full-page photos:

Finding. On a clean whole page both single-location marks are strong: the header serial and the 2 cm QR were read 12/12 at phone quality and under WhatsApp compression. They fail where the fingerprint does not — blur σ=2.5 (header 1/12, QR 5/12), 600 px width (3/12, 0/12), the hard WhatsApp case (1/12, 2/12) — and, above all, when the crop leaves the mark out (§4.3). Fingerprint vs. baseline is therefore a robustness-to-quality-and-cropping argument, not an accuracy argument on good full-page photos.

4.2b Offset size vs printer resolution

Nominal photo, 0.05 pt per-word placement noise, bilevel printing at 1200/600/300/150 dpi (one dot = 0.06/0.12/0.24/0.48 pt). Full page and 6-line crop (8 trials per cell):

Finding. Offsets far below one printer dot still decode, because a word's many ink edges snap to the dot grid independently and the average shift survives. A 6-line crop at 0.10 pt / 600 dpi was the only miss (7/8). This is a simulation property: real toner spread, paper texture and motion blur are structured, not independent, noise and are what the real-photo protocol must measure.

Finding. At phone quality the smallest crop reaching ≥90% is 4–6 lines (pooled over both runs: 25/28 at 4 lines, CI 73–96%; 100% from 6 lines); 3 lines are correctly identified before the significance test in 14/14 trials but only 29% (v1.1) / 14% (v2) clear α=10-3 — exactly the information floor of §2.2 (≈19 bits needed, ≈15 available). For the low-resolution WhatsApp-style photo, crops of ≤4 lines yield a median of only 0–18 measurable positions — the OCR cannot read ~5 px text, so the failure is alignment, not statistics — and 12 lines give 86%; ≥90% needs about 20 lines. The decoder's wrong-key σ falls with the number of visible positions M as M-0.48 (theory −0.50, R²=0.94.), confirming the 1/√M behaviour.

A mark in one place survives only when the crop happens to include it and the photo is sharp enough to read it; a leaker who crops to the questions removes it by construction, while the fingerprint does not depend on where the crop lies. Multi-scale OCR (v2) did not help measurably (hard, 6 lines: 57% v1.1 vs 50% v2 on fresh trials; CIs overlap): the hard-quality limit is the photo's resolution.

Disclosure — a bug found and fixed. The first E3 run used a decoder whose rotation fallback overwrote the upright OCR anchors of tiny crops. After the fix the hard-quality 6-line accuracy went from 14% to 57%. The buggy run is kept in outputs/e3_archive_rotation_bug/; all numbers above are from the fixed decoder and a QR baseline enlarged from 1 cm to 2 cm after it proved unrealistically small.

Finding. On full pages and 6-line crops Hindi is as accurate as English (100% in all full-page conditions; 0 plain-page false accepts in 24 each). Script-specific differences are measurable: (i) OCR anchors — Tesseract-hin recovers a median of 170 of ≈363 words per page against 304 of ≈352 for English; (ii) per-gap measurement error is larger for Devanagari (RMSE 0.34–0.36 vs 0.28–0.32, ≈1.1–1.3×; up to 1.6× for words under 15 pt: 0.19 vs 0.12), plausibly because the headline (shirorekha) and dense matras give less horizontal structure per patch — a hypothesis, not tested; (iii) at 3 lines every Hindi trial was identified correctly before the significance test (12/12) but none cleared α=10-3 (z 3.3–4.3 vs the 4.4 threshold), because 12 pt Hindi lines hold fewer words and hence fewer marked gaps (24–40 vs 22–52 per 3 lines). The Hindi shortfall at short crops is an information-content effect, not a decoding failure.

Findings. (1) Photo-level transformations — rescaling to 20% and back, JPEG q15, median filtering, unsharp masking, halving the contrast, 10° and 90°/180° rotation — did not change identification. (2) 30° rotation failed (0/12) with decoder v1.1 because Tesseract could not read steeply skewed lines. A skew estimate before OCR (decoder v2, fresh trials, table right) fixed it: 60/60 correct at 15°, ±30° and ±45°. This fix was designed after seeing the failure, so the fresh trials, not the original ones, are the evidence. (3) Collusion: the top-ranked centre was always a colluder (48/48), innocent centres entered the strict set 0 times, and averaged copies were fully recovered 10–12/12 times; but for three colluders mixing line-by-line only 1/12 strict and 4/12 lead sets contained all three (11/12 contained at least one). Recovering every colluder in that case needs segment-wise (per-line) attribution, which is not implemented. (4) Noise injection: adding random per-word jitter up to σ=0.4 pt (larger than δ) still left 12/12 correct; σ=0.8 pt destroyed the fingerprint (1/12) — at that size the paper is visibly damaged but an adversary with the PDF could do it. (5) Retyping removes the fingerprint (documented limit): retyped text in the same template or in a different font size/line height was never accepted (0/12 and 0/9) — the lead is lost, not misattributed.

5 Real printed-and-photographed evidence (not yet collected)

data/photos/README.md specifies the protocol: python -m eval.real_photos pack writes one fingerprinted PDF per centre plus a plain control; print on a laser printer at 100% (never fit-to-page), photograph every page with 2–3 phones at 25/40/60 cm, 0/15/30°, three lighting conditions, whole page and cropped to ~3/6/12 lines, send a random half through WhatsApp, label every photo in labels.csv (printer, paper, phone, distance, angle, lighting, crop, WhatsApp, true centre), then run python -m eval.real_photos run for accuracy and false-accept tables by factor with Wilson intervals. Folder layout (originals/, whatsapp/, labels.csv) and a three-row example are included. Until this is done every accuracy above is a simulation result.

6 Limitations

  • Simulation only. The simulator's noise is largely independent per pixel and per word. Printer feed error, toner spread, paper curl, lens distortion, rolling shutter and hand shake are modelled coarsely and may be worse in practice; sub-pixel measurement depends on them.
  • Visibility is unmeasured. No human result exists; 0.30 pt is a placeholder. A larger δ is more robust and more likely to be noticed; the study decides.
  • Retyping and re-typesetting remove the mark; so do OCR-copy-and-reprint workflows. A photo of a retyped paper is rejected, giving no lead.
  • Information floor. About 4 readable lines are needed for a strict (α=10-3) decision over 200 centres, more with more centres (5000 centres: z ≥ 4.9, ≈24 bits); fewer lines give only a ranked lead.
  • Alignment relies on OCR. Low-resolution, blurred or heavily skewed text defeats it (hard-quality crops under ~12 lines; steep rotation unless the v2 skew step is used, which is only validated to ±45°). Hindi OCR yields roughly half the anchors English does.
  • Collusion: one colluder is reliably found, the complete set not always (3-way line mixing).
  • Paper source. Papers must be typeset by LeakTrace (our JSON or plain-text input); arbitrary supplied PDFs/Word files cannot be re-flowed with offsets. Left-aligned (non-justified) text works the same way but was not separately evaluated; only A4 portrait text with no figures was tested.
  • Statistics. 8–16 trials per cell; no multiple-comparison correction across cells; false-accept rate at α=10-3 not empirically resolvable with ≤160 negatives. The decoder's few constants (patch margins, quality mapping, trend orders) were set on a development key and a handful of photos, not on the reported trials, but two decoder defects were found after seeing results and are disclosed above.
  • Evidence and ethics. The output is a statistical lead that must be corroborated; it cannot identify who photographed or posted a paper, only which printed copy. Misuse risks (false suspicion of a centre) argue for always showing the p-value, the margin and the “not proof” notice, as the dashboard does. Only invented mock papers were used; the reader study is anonymous and needs approval.

7 Reproduce

make setup test e1 study e2 e3 e4 e5, then python -m eval.e2b_printer, python -m eval.e5_rotation_v2 and python docs/build_report.py. Raw per-trial results: outputs/*/*.jsonl. App: make api and make web. Repository map and run commands: README.md.
